content: Chemical reactions involve the breaking and forming of bonds between atoms to create new substances with different properties. In baking, ingredients undergo various reactions triggered by heat, moisture, and mixing. The Maillard reaction occurs when proteins (amino acids) react with sugars under heat, creating brown colors and complex flavors on cookie surfaces. This non-enzymatic browning differs from caramelization, which involves the pyrolysis of sugars alone at higher temperatures (>300Â°F). Leavening agents like baking soda (sodium bicarbonate, NaHCOâ) undergo decomposition reactions when heated, producing carbon dioxide gas that causes cookies to rise: 2NaHCOâ â NaâCOâ + HâO + COâ. Baking powder contains both an acid and baking soda, allowing the acid-base reaction to produce COâ even before heating. Fats like butter undergo physical state changes during baking, first melting and spreading, then allowing water to evaporate, and finally enabling structural setting through protein coagulation. Chemical reaction rates increase with temperature according to the Arrhenius equation, explaining why cookies bake faster at higher oven temperatures.

scenario.title: Cookie Chemistry Lab
scenario.content: Students experiment in a virtual kitchen where they select, measure, and combine ingredients to create cookies with specific characteristics. The simulation visualizes molecular interactions during mixing and baking, showing how different ingredients and processes affect chemical reactions. Students can adjust variables like temperature, ingredient ratios, mixing methods, and baking time to observe their impact on final results. The simulation highlights key reactions like Maillard browning, caramelization, and leavening in real-time, allowing students to see normally invisible processes. Challenge modes ask students to troubleshoot cookie failures or optimize recipes for particular traits like chewiness, crispness, or resistance to spreading.

hypothesis.description: Students will analyze chemical reactions by examining how ingredients interact under various conditions. They will predict how changes in reactants, temperature, and process affect reaction outcomes, and apply this understanding to design optimal conditions for desired results.
